items.title: Prof Bokpin urges transparency on ECG reforms, warns of fiscal risks
items.description: Economist and Professor of Finance, Prof. Godfred Bokpin, has called for greater transparency and broader national consultation over proposed reforms in Ghana’s electricity sector, warning that the persistent financial challenges facing the Electricity Company of Ghana (ECG) continue to pose a major risk to the country’s fiscal stability. Speaking on JoyNews’ Newsfile on Saturday, Prof Bokpin said the structural problems confronting Ghana’s energy sector did not originate with the current International Monetary Fund (IMF)-supported programme. He argued that issues including inefficiencies, losses across the electricity value chain, weak revenue collection and the financial obligations associated with power generation and distribution had existed for decades. According to him, the IMF programme has nevertheless helped bring greater transparency to the sector and has provided a framework within which some of the long-standing problems can be better measured and addressed. “The issues that have been identified as the root causes have been with us for years, for decades, even before this IMF-supported programme,” Prof Bokpin said. He stressed that the continuing challenges should therefore not be interpreted simply as failures of the current IMF programme, but rather as evidence of structural weaknesses that successive governments have struggled to resolve. Prof Bokpin said the energy sector had been identified as one of the major fiscal risks under Ghana’s IMF-supported programme and maintained that the risk remains significant. He said while the government and its partners now have better information about the scale of the sector’s problems, the underlying financial pressures have not disappeared. “The energy-sector risk was a big issue. It was a big issue and it is still a big issue,” he said. The economist cautioned against dismissing or attacking data showing the amount of money required to settle obligations within the sector. He said projections concerning payments and liabilities should instead be used to understand the extent of the problem and assess whether reforms are delivering tangible improvements. “The data they are referring to here, what needs to be paid, the projections, these are not good data to bastardise the sector. No, not at all,” he said. He argued, the more important development under the IMF programme has been the increased transparency surrounding the sector’s financial position, including the scale of losses and the progress being made in addressing them. Prof Bokpin identified the cash waterfall mechanism as one area where he believes the IMF-supported reforms have produced some improvement. The mechanism is intended to ensure that revenues collected within the electricity sector are distributed according to an agreed priority structure, allowing payments to be made to key participants in the electricity supply chain. According to Prof Bokpin, the mechanism is now functioning to some extent, representing an improvement over the situation that existed before the IMF programme. “Today, the cash waterfall mechanism is working to some extent. You can credit that to the IMF programme because we know what was happening with the cash waterfall mechanism before,” he said. He suggested that such improvements in transparency and financial discipline should be recognised even as the country continues to grapple with the sector’s deeper structural challenges. Despite these improvements, Prof Bokpin expressed concern about the amount of public money required to sustain the energy sector. He said the additional budgetary allocations needed to support the sector had become so significant that they could exceed the combined allocations to some of Ghana’s key social and economic sectors. “If you look at the fiscal space that the energy sector alone takes, the extra-budgetary allocation that we have to make to cover the energy sector also exceeds the combined budgetary allocation to the Ministry of Health, Food and Agriculture, Education,” he said. His comments underline the difficult choices facing the government as it attempts to maintain reliable electricity supply while simultaneously protecting scarce public resources for health, education, agriculture and other development priorities. Prof Bokpin questioned whether Ghana could continue to address the problem primarily through government funding. He said successive administrations had failed over the decades to implement the necessary reforms without significant political and institutional constraints. “Are we able to implement this on our own? We have not. Over the decades, we have not,” he said. The economist also stressed that reducing losses across Ghana’s electricity value chain would require significant investment. He said the country could not expect substantial improvements in generation, transmission and distribution efficiency without investing in the infrastructure and systems needed to reduce technical and commercial losses. “There’s no way we can reduce the level of losses from generation, transmission to distribution without a certain level of investment,” Prof Bokpin said. The challenge, he noted, is determining how that investment should be financed. If government is expected to provide all the necessary funding, he argued, it could place even greater pressure on the national budget and reduce the resources available to other sectors. The central question, therefore, is how Ghana can close the investment gap while ensuring that the required improvements in efficiency actually materialise. Prof Bokpin noted that government had increased allocations through the Ministry of Finance over the past four to five years, but maintained that additional public spending must be accompanied by measurable improvements in efficiency and performance. A significant part of Prof Bokpin’s argument centred on the proposed involvement of private-sector operators in ECG and the electricity distribution sector. He questioned whether the government had sufficiently explained to Ghanaians exactly what it means by private-sector participation. “There are various forms of private-sector participation. Which form are they going for?” he asked. Prof Bokpin said the current discussion could easily be interpreted by the public as an attempt to hand ECG entirely to private investors. However, he argued that private-sector participation does not necessarily mean transferring the entire electricity value chain to private companies. One possible model, he suggested, could involve ECG remaining as a holding company while private operators take responsibility for distribution in designated geographical zones. Under such an arrangement, private companies could purchase electricity from ECG, distribute it to consumers and collect payments, subsequently paying ECG according to an agreed commercial arrangement. He said this model could allow private-sector operators to contribute capital, expertise and operational efficiency without necessarily taking over the entire electricity system. “ECG probably is going to be a holding company. There’s going to be maybe four or three or so different private-sector companies,” he said. Prof Bokpin stressed, however, that the government needs to disclose its intended structure clearly before the reforms are implemented. The economist also pointed to Ghana’s previous experience with private-sector involvement in electricity distribution and revenue collection. He said there had been evidence of improved revenue collection when private operators became involved in aspects of ECG’s operations. “We know that there was some level of improvement when EDS took over immediately with collection and all of that,” he said. However, he stressed that Ghana does not necessarily have to replicate the previous arrangement exactly. Instead, lessons from that experience should inform a new model that is better designed and adapted to the country’s current circumstances. For Prof Bokpin, the critical issues are transparency, accountability, effective regulation and ensuring that the proposed arrangement delivers measurable improvements in efficiency. Prof Bokpin also argued that the energy-sector reforms should be approached as a national rather than partisan issue. He pointed out that both of Ghana’s two major political parties have played roles in the evolution of private-sector participation in the energy sector. He said the IMF programme was negotiated by the previous NPP administration, which agreed to the reforms, while the current NDC administration inherited the programme and has also accepted the principle that greater private-sector participation is necessary to address the challenges confronting the sector. He therefore called for a broader consultation involving political parties, organised labour, industry stakeholders and the wider Ghanaian public. “The IMF programme was negotiated by the NPP administration and they agreed to these reforms, which the NDC has inherited,” he said. He added that the NDC administration also recognises private-sector participation as an important component of efforts to address losses across generation, transmission and distribution. According to Prof Bokpin, the shared position of the two major political parties creates an opportunity to build a more durable national consensus around the reforms. Prof Bokpin cautioned against presenting the proposed reforms as though private investors would take control of the entire electricity value chain. He said the government could explore a model under which ECG remains publicly owned while private companies operate specific distribution zones. Such an arrangement, he suggested, could allow Ghana to retain strategic oversight of the electricity sector while leveraging private-sector capital and expertise to improve distribution and revenue collection. He said the details of the proposal must, however, be made public. “There has to be greater disclosure of what kind of private-sector participation we are talking about,” he said. Without such disclosure, he warned, public uncertainty and political resistance could undermine the reform process. Prof Bokpin placed the ECG challenge within the broader problem of inefficiencies among Ghana’s state-owned enterprises. He said the government’s proposed policy-coordination reforms were largely focused on improving the performance of state-owned enterprises, which he argued have imposed a significant cost on the economy over many years. “Over the last 15, 20 years, between 2.5% to almost 3.2% of our GDP is lost to the inefficiencies of state-owned enterprises alone, including ECG and then Cocoa Board and the rest of them,” he said. He warned that continuing with the existing approach could undermine Ghana’s fiscal recovery and eventually force the country to seek another round of external financial assistance. “If we go back to business as usual, it’s just a matter of time and we have to resort to the IMF and the World Bank for another level of intervention,” he cautioned. Prof Bokpin also highlighted the government’s commitment under its policy framework to conclude the private-sector participation process by June 2027. He noted that previous administrations had also set reform targets for the energy sector, but implementation had been slowed by political considerations, including electoral cycles. He suggested that the reforms must now be insulated from short-term political calculations if Ghana is to achieve lasting improvements. According to him, the country’s fiscal position means that postponing difficult decisions is no longer a sustainable option. He argued that Ghana cannot continue to accumulate energy-sector liabilities, inject public funds into inefficient state-owned enterprises and expect the same model to deliver a different outcome. He warned that when ECG and other entities within the electricity value chain operate inefficiently, the cost is ultimately transferred to consumers through tariffs, taxes and the wider economic consequences of fiscal pressures. “We cannot continue as business as usual, the way we have done things, because really, the consumer will continue to pay and pay and pay and will not get far,” he said.

items.title: NPP constituency primaries: Annulment of initial election was unnecessary, but party decision must stand – Bantama MP
items.description: The Member of Parliament for Bantama Constituency, Francis Asenso-Boakye, has expressed disappointment over the New Patriotic Party’s decision to annul the initial constituency executive elections held on July 11, 2026. Speaking to JoyNews after casting his ballot in the re-run election at the Kumasi Cultural Centre, the MP said he did not see the need for the NPP’s National Steering Committee to take such a decision, adding that the process of the initial election was transparent. “I am disappointed that we had to come back and do this all over again. The first election was conducted peacefully, just as the ongoing one,” the MP stated. The MP said that despite his reservations, he supports the decision to re-conduct the election because it is the party’s directive. “Even though I am disappointed, I am also in support of the re-run of the election since it is the party’s decision to re-conduct the election,” he noted. Mr. Asenso-Boakye also acknowledged what he described as a fair and orderly process in the ongoing re-run after touring all three voting centers at the venue. “I have moved around all the voting centers and I can say that the process so far has been peaceful and transparent. Delegates are voting without any interference,” he said. The MP further assured that he will work closely with whoever is elected by the party delegates, stressing that unity is key to securing victory for the party’s flagbearer, Dr. Mahamudu Bawumia, in the 2028 general elections. “For me it’s about party unity. We will all rally behind the winners and work hard for Dr. Bawumia’s victory in 2028,” he added. Background The re-run comes after the NPP’s National Steering Committee annulled the initial poll held on July 11, citing breaches of party directives, electoral regulations, and in some cases, existing court orders. In contrast to the first exercise, which was held without Electoral Commission oversight and was disrupted, Sunday’s re-run is being supervised by officials from the EC. A total of 1,258 delegates are expected to vote at the Kumasi Cultural Centre to elect new constituency executives to lead the party’s activities in Bantema ahead of the 2028 general elections. Security personnel from the Ghana Police Service have been deployed to the venue to maintain law and order. The process, scheduled to end at 4pm, is being closely monitored by national and regional party executives to ensure strict adherence to the NPP’s constitution and electoral guidelines.

items.title: Pakistan, New Zealand seek to boost cooperation in agri, education sectors
items.description: Pakistan and New Zealand discussed boosting cooperation in various fields, with a special focus on agriculture and education, as the two sides held a Joint Trade Committee (JTC) meeting in Wellington, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Saturday. The third Pakistan-New Zealand JTC meeting and the fifth round of Pakistan-New Zealand Political Consultations were held in Wellington on Thursday, “marking a significant step in deepening bilateral engagement between the two countries”, the FO said. A key outcome of the meetings was the signing of the Education Cooperation Arrangement between Pakistan and New Zealand, which is “expected to significantly deepen collaboration in the education sector”. At the JTC meeting, both sides “deliberated on improving market access and enhancing cooperation in sustainable agriculture, including exploring technical collaboration in wool production and plant protection”, the FO said. The discussions focused on bolstering bilateral trade and investment, with particular emphasis on technology, education and services. Institutional mechanisms to further economic cooperation were also discussed, the statement added. Commerce Secretary Jawad Paul Khawaja represented Pakistan during the JTC meeting, while Grahame Morton, deputy secretary of the Americas and Asia Group at New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, headed the other delegation. Meanwhile, during the political consultations, both sides conducted a comprehensive review of bilateral relations. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments, and agreed to enhance coordination within multilateral forums. Additional Foreign Secretary (Asia Pacific) Ambassador Dr Syed Ali Asad Gillani co-chaired the Pakistani side at the political consultations, while Morton headed the New Zealand delegation. Islamabad and Wellington “explored avenues to strengthen cooperation across a wide spectrum of areas of mutual interest, including high-level exchanges, economic development, science and technology, education, counterterrorism, transnational crime, and people-to-people ties”, the FO said. Ambassador Gillani briefed the New Zealand side on Pakistan’s efforts to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East, as Islamabad remains actively engaged in efforts to defuse the Strait of Hormuz stand-off. Morton “acknowledged Pakistan’s constructive role in the Middle East peace process”, the FO statement said. Gillani also discussed the situation in South Asia, including in India-occupied Kashmir (IoK) and India’s “ continued violations ” of the Indus Waters Treaty (IWT). India had unilaterally decided to put the IWT in abeyance in late April 2025 after hostilities flared up between the two neighbours last year. The issue of water has remained a bitter point of contention between the nuclear-armed nations since then, with Islamabad repeatedly raising the issue on international platforms. The overall discussions between Pakistan and New Zealand “provided an opportunity to assess progress in bilateral ties, identify new areas for partnership, and reaffirm the shared commitment to a forward-looking and mutually beneficial relationship”, the FO noted. Pakistan and New Zealand enjoy cordial and friendly relations, with both countries being members of the Commonwealth. Bilateral trade stands at $12 million, with Pakistan’s major exports being textile products, apparel, rice, leather articles and sports goods, according to the FO’s website . Main imports from New Zealand include dairy products, wood pulp, paper, edible oil, wood, iron steel and electrical machinery. Agriculture and education were also among areas of cooperation discussed between the two sides when former military dictator Gen Pervez Musharraf visited Auckland in June 2005. Last month, India and New Zealand signed a free trade deal as they sought to boost exports amid global economic uncertainty made worse by the war in the Middle East.

items.title: Déraillement d’un train à Alger : trafic ferroviaire perturbé
items.description: Un train de transport de voyageurs a déraillé ce samedi 8 août entre les gares ferroviaires de Gué de Constantine et d’El Harrach à Alger, a indiqué la Société nationale des transports ferroviaires (SNTF). Ce déraillement perturbe la circulation des trains entre Thenia et Zeralda. La SNTF a annoncé un réaménagement du programme de circulation des trains de banlieue, précisant que la gare de Bab Ali sera la dernière destination du voyage, sans préciser dans quel sens. Ce changement est valable « jusqu'à la fin des opérations d'intervention et la réouverture de la ligne à la circulation ferroviaire. » La SNTF assure que ses équipes « d'intervention et de maintenance poursuivent sans relâche leurs travaux sur le terrain afin de préparer la reprise du trafic ferroviaire et le retour à un fonctionnement normal dans les meilleurs délais. » Elle affirme qu’elle tiendra au courant les voyageurs de « toute évolution concernant la reprise du trafic et le retour aux horaires habituels ». La SNTF n’a pas fait état de victimes, ni de dégâts matériels. Elle n’a pas précisé si le train qui a déraillé transportait des voyageurs ou non. Les raisons de cet accident ferroviaire n’ont pas été précisées. L’article Déraillement d’un train à Alger : trafic ferroviaire perturbé est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Nécrologie : Djibril Dièye, l’animateur d’« Auto Mag » sur la TFM, s’est éteint
items.description: Le paysage médiatique sénégalais est en deuil. Djibril Dièye, animateur emblématique de « Auto Mag » sur la TFM, a perdu son combat contre la maladie, suscitant un élan de solidarité et une collecte de fonds pour sa prise en charge médicale durant ses dernières années. Il est décédé vendredi 7 août 2026. L'annonce a été faite à l'antenne par Bouba Ndour, directeur des programmes de la TFM, au cours de l'émission « Jakkaarloo » vendredi soir. Selon les précisions apportées par plusieurs médias, l'animateur était malade depuis plusieurs années et son état de santé s'était fortement dégradé au fil du temps, au point de l’empêcher de s'exprimer normalement. Une mobilisation citoyenne autour de sa maladie Face à cette dégradation, un mouvement de solidarité s'était organisé autour de lui. Une cagnotte avait été mise en place par des citoyens afin de contribuer à son évacuation à l'étranger pour y recevoir des soins. Cette mobilisation témoignait de l'attachement du public à un animateur devenu, au fil des années, une figure familière du petit écran. Une passion pour l'automobile qui a marqué le public Djibril Dièye s'était fait connaître à travers « Auto Mag », une émission consacrée à l'univers automobile qui avait fidélisé de nombreux téléspectateurs. Sa capacité à transmettre sa passion pour ce secteur lui avait valu une reconnaissance particulière auprès des amateurs de voitures au Sénégal. Malgré la gravité de son état, des signaux d'espoir avaient ponctué ces derniers mois notamment l'annonce de son mariage en janvier 2025, un moment vécu comme un motif d'optimisme par ses proches et ses admirateurs. Sa disparition laisse un vide important, tant auprès de ses collègues de la TFM que des passionnés d'automobile qui suivaient fidèlement son émission. La rédaction présente ses condoléances à sa famille, à ses proches et à l'ensemble du personnel de la Télévision Futurs Médias. C.G.D

items.title: Lutte antiterroriste : Le comité de gestion du Fonds de soutien patriotique constate l’impact de ses investissements aux VDP dans la région du Goulmou
items.description: Une délégation du Fonds de soutien patriotique (FSP) s’est rendue à Fada N’Gourma, dans la région du Goulmou, le vendredi 7 août 2026. Cette immersion sur le terrain visait à permettre aux membres du Conseil d’orientation et du Comité de gestion du FSP d’évaluer concrètement les réalisations et les moyens déployés en faveur des Volontaires pour la défense de la patrie (VDP). Accueillie par le Gouverneur de la région du Goulmou et accompagnée par la Brigade de veille et de défense patriotique (BVDP), la délégation a notamment visité le Bataillon mixte de marche Fantôme 1 et 2. La délégation était conduite par le secrétaire général du FSP, Vieux Abdoul Rachid Soulama Selon le secrétaire général du FSP, Vieux Abdoul Rachid Soulama, cette visite répond à une instruction du Premier ministre, président du Conseil d’orientation du FSP. L’objectif est de permettre aux instances du fonds de mieux apprécier, sur le terrain, l’utilisation des ressources mobilisées. Des équipements de grande envergure Au cours de cette visite, la délégation a pu constater l’acquisition d’un important lot de logistique et d’armement, ainsi que de tentes individuelles destinées à chaque VDP. Elle a également observé les moyens roulants financés par le FSP, composés notamment de motos Aloba, dont certaines ont été adaptées aux contraintes du terrain, de tricycles ordinaires ou modifiés, de pick-up et d’ambulances. Vieux Abdoul Rachid Soulama mobilisant les soldats Par ailleurs, les visiteurs ont découvert l’infirmerie aménagée au sein du bataillon, équipée de kits de premiers secours et dotée d’infirmiers et d’aides-soignants issus des rangs des VDP. À l’issue de la visite, Vieux Abdoul Rachid Soulama, représentant du président du Conseil d’orientation du FSP, s’est déclaré satisfait des réalisations constatées. « Nous sommes vraiment émerveillés par ce qui a été fait, par les résultats qui nous ont été présentés et par les perspectives. Surtout, nous avons pu constater de visu le travail gigantesque accompli », a-t-il affirmé. Du matériel acquis grâce au FSP Vieux Abdoul Rachid Soulama a souligné que les ressources du FSP contribuent de manière décisive à l’opérationnalisation et au fonctionnement du bataillon. « Les matériels que nous venons de voir, notamment les armements, les moyens roulants et les équipements adaptés à chaque VDP, représentent un investissement évalué à près d’un milliard de francs CFA », a-t-il précisé. Le secrétaire général du FSP a également indiqué que les dépenses mensuelles consacrées à la prise en charge des VDP de ce bataillon s’élèvent à plus de 700 millions de francs CFA, couvrant l’entretien des hommes, la santé, les primes et l’alimentation. Une satisfaction partagée par les bénéficiaires La délégation a également constaté que des actions de renforcement du bataillon sont en cours, notamment à travers la formation de plusieurs centaines de VDP. Des tentes individuelles pour les VDP Le commandant de la BVDP, le lieutenant-colonel Mahamadi Sawadogo, a souligné que ces efforts témoignent de l’importance de la contribution des Burkinabè au FSP. « Chaque franc injecté dans le Fonds de soutien patriotique contribue à renforcer les capacités opérationnelles de nos VDP et de nos forces de défense et de sécurité sur le terrain », a-t-il déclaré. Lors de la visite, la délégation a pu observer également la restauration servie aux hommes qui combattent pour la reconquête du territoire national. Plaisantant sur le menu du jour, le commandant de la BVDP a lancé : « Vous voyez, secrétaire général, ce plat, riche en minéraux et en vitamines, est l’un des grands bienfaits du FSP. Nous ne cesserons de saluer l’élan des populations. Nous les invitons à continuer à nous soutenir, car chaque franc qu’elles versent contribue à nourrir efficacement nos hommes sur le terrain ». Visite dans une infirmerie des VDP Un appel renouvelé à la mobilisation Au regard des résultats observés à Fada N’Gourma, la délégation a renouvelé son appel à la mobilisation autour du FSP. Elle a, par ailleurs, félicité la BVDP, les VDP et le personnel d’encadrement pour le travail accompli. Selon le représentant du Conseil d’orientation du FSP, cette immersion a permis de mesurer concrètement l’impact des ressources mobilisées et de constater les efforts engagés pour renforcer les capacités opérationnelles sur le terrain. Les bénéficiaires de ces fonds ont d’ailleurs témoigné leur satisfaction à l’égard de la délégation par des chants, des danses et des cris de joie. Un aperçu des soldats Créé le 23 janvier 2023, le FSP a pour mission de financer et d’intensifier la lutte contre le terrorisme au Burkina Faso, d’assurer la prise en charge et l’équipement des VDP, et de renforcer la souveraineté financière de l’armée nationale face à l’insuffisance des aides extérieures. Au premier trimestre 2026, les recettes mobilisées en sa faveur ont atteint plus de 45 milliards de francs CFA, en hausse de 28 % par rapport à la même période en 2025. Lire aussi : Fonds de soutien patriotique : Près de 500 milliards mobilisés en trois ans Nadège KINDA Minute.bf

items.title: Diapaga : marché central et caniveaux assainis dans la lutte contre le paludisme
items.description: Diapaga : marché central et caniveaux assainis dans la lutte contre le paludisme Diapaga, 8 août 2026 (AIB)-En réponse à l'offensive de lutte pour la destruction des gîtes larvaires, placée sous le thème « Ne soyons plus complices des moustiques, détruisons les gîtes larvaires », la délégation spéciale de Diapaga, en tandem avec le district sanitaire de Diapaga, a ciblé ce 8 août à Diapaga les caniveaux et le marché central pour répondre à cette initiative du gouvernement. Procéder à la réduction de la transmission du paludisme et d'autres maladies (dengue, diarrhée) par l'élimination régulière des gîtes larvaires et l'assainissement durable de l'environnement, c'est dans cette optique qu'il faut situer cette journée dont le top de départ a été donné ce samedi 8 août à Diapaga, par la délégation spéciale de Diapaga, en tandem avec le district sanitaire de Diapaga. Dès 6 h 30, les forces vives de Diapaga, qui n'ont pas monnayé leur déplacement, ont pris d'assaut les sites ciblés pour des activités d'ordre communautaire, afin d'assainir le cadre de vie et de prévenir les maladies susmentionnées. Munis de pelles, râteaux et brouettes, les forces vives de Diapaga ont procédé au curage des caniveaux, à la destruction des potentiels gîtes larvaires, à l'enlèvement des ordures et, dans un élan patriotique, ont également géré les dépotoirs sauvages, ainsi qu'à la sensibilisation sur la nécessité d'assainir notre cadre de vie. Les jours à venir, des opérations d'enlèvement des dépôts d'ordures sauvages seront organisées pour les convoyer hors de la ville. Pour le camarade président de la délégation spéciale, Yambi Bamogo, les populations de Diapaga refusent d'être complices des moustiques : « Nous devons rendre notre ville propre et saine pour nous et pour nos enfants. » Il a ensuite invité chaque ménage, chaque boutique, chaque service à s'approprier cette lutte, car un environnement propre, c'est une vie sauvée du paludisme et de la dengue. Pour le docteur Bazié, représentant le médecin-chef du district sanitaire, le paludisme et la dengue tuent encore au Burkina. « Avec cette saison hivernale, les eaux stagnantes dans les caniveaux et les ordures deviennent des gîtes à moustiques », a-t-il indiqué. Selon toujours le docteur Bazié, 70 % des cas de paludisme viennent de notre environnement. « Si nous assainissons, nous coupons la chaîne de transmission », a conclu le camarade docteur Bazié. Agence d'Information du Burkina LBK/Ata

items.title: Chine, la fascinante innovation (Par Daouda MANÉ)
items.description: Nous le rappelions souvent. Il n’y a pas d’alternative à la recherche. Car, dans le monde actuel, une chose est sûre : seule l’innovation, qui a propulsé des pays comme la Corée du Sud au rang des pays riches, peut favoriser un développement accéléré et harmonieux. C’est la voie que doit emprunter le Sénégal, en plus de la formation professionnelle, pour espérer se développer. Faudrait-il le rappeler, l’innovation est au cœur du développement des États asiatiques comme la Chine, devenue une puissance inégalée en matière d’innovation. Dans ce domaine, la Chine ne semble plus avoir de limites. Elle a si accéléré la cadence qu’elle inquiète les pays occidentaux. Jadis, accusée de pays « copieur » ou d’exportateur de « faux produits », la Chine a fait de grands bonds en avant dans l’innovation. C’est dans cette optique qu’il faut comprendre la mesure inédite – ce, après la mesure qui a consisté à supprimer certaines formations dans les universités – consistant à permettre à certains doctorants en ingénierie de valider leur diplôme grâce à un produit, un prototype ou une innovation technologique au lieu de rédiger une longue thèse académique. La mesure qui cible les filières techniques et stratégiques vise à stimuler l’industrie. Ce basculement, selon Netafrique, vers le « doctorat pratique » est le fruit d’une modification de la loi en janvier 2025, légalisant le dispositif qui couvait depuis 2010 sous le nom de « Engineers Plan ». Et d’après les chiffres, plus de 20.000 étudiants sont inscrits dans ce cursus d’élite, répartis dans 60 universités de premier plan et connectés à plus de 100 entreprises partenaires. L’objectif ? Transformer les campus en laboratoires industriels géants où la recherche doit impérativement déboucher sur une solution matérielle immédiate. (Cf. https://netafrique.net du 16 juillet 2026). C’est pourquoi, d’après media24fr, l’Empire du Milieu parvient à construire des réacteurs nucléaires en 62 mois, dominant ainsi l’énergie nucléaire avec le réacteur Hualong One surnommé le HPR-1000 à l’international, champion mondial du nucléaire de 3e génération. Chaque unité peut produire de l’électricité pour au moins un million de personnes. En fait, le pays est devenu le premier en matière d’innovation. En témoigne le nombre de brevets que l’Empire du Milieu dépose par an. À en croire Mathias Baccino, dirigeant de Fintech (Trade Republic, la première plateforme d’épargne en Europe) et pédagogue, en 2024, la Chine a déposé 1,8 million de brevets contre 500.000 pour les États-Unis, 400.000 pour le Japon, 50.000 pour la France qui est 7e. Mieux, poursuit Bccino, la Chine s’est dotée d’un nouveau plan de développement qui veut faire passer les industries numériques de 10,5 à 12,5 % du Pib d’ici à 2030 et surtout le pays veut maintenir ses dépenses de recherche et de développement à 7% du Pib, contre 2 % en France. Il a également 3 fois plus de Recherche-développement que la France. C’est dire qu’en termes d’innovation, la Chine est en train de dépasser très largement la plupart des pays occidentaux. Ce que ces derniers considèrent comme une « menace considérable ». Surtout que l’Empire du Milieu, dans sa quête de construction du monde de demain, a décidé d’accélérer dans « 10 secteurs industriels que sont les semi-conducteurs, les robots humanoïdes, la science du vivant, les batteries de nouvelle génération, les fusées réutilisables, l’aéronautique, les drones, l’hydrogène vert, les interfaces cerveau machine et les équipements médicaux », dixit Baccino. Il a également listé « 6 industries du futur sur lesquelles il veut prendre le leadership : la quantique, la fusion nucléaire, la 6G, les interfaces cerveau machine, l’IA embarquée et le biomanufacturing, c’est-à-dire le fait de fabriquer tout simplement du vivant ». En outre, la Chine souhaite faire « 8 percées technologiques : Supercalculateur et algorithme d’IA, l’ordinateur quantique, la fusion nucléaire, la biotech et le génome, le traitement des maladies, l’exploration polaire, marine et spatiale ainsi que les neurosciences ». En réalité, la Chine investit massivement dans plusieurs secteurs-clés que sont l’innovation, l’industrie, les infrastructures et les technologies du futur afin de vite rattraper son retard voire dépasser de loin ses concurrents. daouda.mane@lesoleil.sn

items.title: Cybersécurité: une alliance propose un registre confidentiel des incidents liés aux agents IA
items.description: La Linux Foundation et l’Open Secure AI Alliance ont ouvert à consultation le projet SAFE, destiné à recueillir les incidents et quasi-accidents impliquant des systèmes d’IA. L’objectif est de produire des tests et des recommandations partagés, sous une gouvernance indépendante qui reste encore à définir. Les entreprises qui déploient des agents d’intelligence artificielle enquêtent souvent seules lorsqu’un système accède à une ressource interdite, divulgue une donnée ou contourne une protection. Le projet Shared AI Findings Exchange, abrégé SAFE, veut créer un mécanisme confidentiel pour tirer des enseignements communs de ces incidents sans publier les informations sensibles des organisations concernées. La Linux Foundation a publié le 4 août une demande de commentaires rédigée avec des membres de l’Open Secure AI Alliance. Cette coalition réunit plus de 120 organisations. Cisco, CrowdStrike, Hugging Face, Nvidia et Red Hat figurent parmi les contributeurs initiaux du texte. La proposition coïncide avec l’ouverture de la conférence de cybersécurité Black Hat à Las Vegas. SAFE couvrirait les incidents avérés et les quasi-accidents. Le dispositif prévoit une collecte confidentielle, une notification rapide des organisations touchées, l’identification des défaillances récurrentes et des analyses portant sur l’ensemble du système : modèle, outils, environnement d’exécution, supervision, opérations humaines et dépendances de la chaîne d’approvisionnement. Les enseignements pourraient être transformés en tests réutilisables, politiques lisibles par des machines, règles de détection, configurations de référence et guides de réponse aux incidents. Le projet s’inspire des systèmes de retour d’expérience utilisés dans l’aviation, où les signalements volontaires servent à prévenir la répétition d’erreurs. Il vise les systèmes propriétaires comme les logiciels ouverts. L’initiative arrive alors que les agents obtiennent davantage de permissions pour consulter des fichiers, appeler des applications et exécuter des tâches. Une erreur de configuration ou une consigne piégée peut alors produire un effet concret sur un compte, un poste de travail ou un service en ligne. Partager des schémas d’incidents aiderait les équipes à corriger plus vite des faiblesses observées chez plusieurs acteurs. SAFE demeure toutefois une proposition soumise à consultation, et non une norme opérationnelle ou une obligation. Les règles de confidentialité, la composition de l’organe indépendant, le financement, la responsabilité juridique et les critères de publication devront être précisés. Le texte prévoit de respecter les contrats et les réglementations existantes; cette précaution pourrait aussi limiter la quantité de données que les entreprises accepteront réellement de partager. Cet article vous est proposé en collaboration avec Aïobi . Contact : team@aiobi.world . L’article Cybersécurité: une alliance propose un registre confidentiel des incidents liés aux agents IA est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Heavy rain disrupts traffic, daily life in Lahore’s low-lying areas
items.description: LAHORE: Heavy rain lashed Lahore on Saturday, inundating low-lying areas, major roads and several underpasses, making movement difficult for pedestrians and motorists in different parts of the city. The downpour disrupted normal traffic as rainwater accumulated on roads and in low-lying localities, leaving motorists struggling to navigate waterlogged stretches. Pedestrians also struggled to move through streets and roads where water had accumulated. According to rainfall data from the Water and Sanitation Agency (Wasa), the city received an average of 24.6mm of rain. The highest rainfall of 104mm was recorded at the airport, followed by 75.6mm at Kahna, 62.6mm at Hadiara Defence Road and 58.6mm at Manawan. Tajpura sub-divisional officer’s (SDO) office recorded 40.2mm of rain, while 32.8mm was recorded at the Mughalpura SDO office. Shadipura received 28.4mm, Nishter Town 28mm, Chowk Nakhuda 11mm, Johar Town SDO Office 11mm, while 10.8mm was recorded at the Wasa head office in Gulberg. Upper Mall received 9mm, Samanabad SDO Office 4.4mm, Iqbal Town SDO Office 3.8mm, Saggian 3.8mm, Lakshmi Chowk 3.2mm, Jail Road 2mm, Gulshan-e-Ravi 1.8mm and Farrukhabad 1.4mm, while only trace rainfall was recorded at Pani Wala Talab. Rain was also reported in Farrukhabad, Tajpura, Defence Phase-VI, Shadipura, Saggian, Lakshmi Chowk, Chowk Nakhuda and surrounding areas. Harbanspura and several other localities received heavy showers. The rain brought relief from the heat and made the weather pleasant, but waterlogging in several areas caused inconvenience to residents and exposed the vulnerability of low-lying localities to heavy rainfall. Meanwhile, Wasa Lahore said it had deployed field staff and machinery at various locations to drain accumulated rainwater. Wasa Managing Director Ghufran Ahmed inspected drainage operations at Mubeen Shaheed Underpass, Noor Jehan Road, MM Alam Road, Main Boulevard Gulberg, Qaddafi Stadium and Liberty Chowk. He also visited Kalma Chowk Underpass, Garden Town Water Tank, Usman Block Emergency Relief Camp and Usman Block Disposal Station. Officials said drainage operations were continuing at waterlogged locations, with heavy machinery deployed in low-lying areas. Disposal stations in areas experiencing power outages were being operated on generators. Wasa Vice Chairman Chaudhry Shehbaz Ahmed also inspected drainage operations at Shalimar Link Road, Bhagwanpura, Baghichi Sethan, UET, Ek Moriya, Do Moriya and Chowk Na Khuda. Earlier, Chief Traffic Officer (CTO) Abdul Rahim Shirazi directed supervisory officers to remain in the field and monitor low-lying points and traffic conditions during the rainfall. Traffic officials were directed to coordinate with Wasa for the timely drainage of rainwater from waterlogged locations. Traffic police advised motorists to drive at moderate speeds, maintain a safe distance from other vehicles and avoid sudden braking on slippery roads. Motorcyclists were advised to wear helmets and avoid unnecessary overtaking. Citizens were also advised to assess the depth of accumulated water before entering flooded roads and avoid crossing stretches where water levels were unsafe. The traffic police warned citizens against standing near electric poles, transformers, fallen power lines, trees, weak walls and under-construction structures during rainfall.

items.title: The Human-Origin Story Is Being Radically Revised
items.description: Some 50,000 years ago, modern humans wandered into Ice Age Europe. The continent was new to us Homo sapiens , but not for beings of our general kind. Neanderthals and their ancestors had been living among Eurasia’s glaciers for ages, and in ways that would have struck us as familiar. Evidence suggests that they may have strung eagle talons together into necklaces and stained their bodily ornaments with pigments . They tended fires, cooked food , and maybe even made their own glue . On sandstone cave walls, they etched wavy lines, dots, and other geometric designs. After first contact, under social circumstances that we cannot possibly imagine, modern humans and Neanderthals had children together; around the same time, in Asia, our species also procreated with another species, the Denisovans. Scientists know this because they have sequenced DNA from Neanderthal and Denisovan remains, and they can see fragments of their code in our genomes to this day. Now we are learning that still more of these fusions of blood and culture may have shaped our lineage. Last week, a team of researchers from UC Berkeley and Johns Hopkins University published new evidence in Science suggesting that two “ghost” ancestors haunt our family tree—not Neanderthals or Denisovans, but some other hominin populations. DNA analysis is only one of the techniques that scientists have been using to cast narrow shafts of light into the dark abyss that is the human past. Researchers from several disciplines have been collecting and reinterpreting ever smaller traces of our forebears to reimagine how they lived, what they made, and what family secrets they might still be hiding. The ghost-ancestors paper is the most recent example. The team from UC Berkeley and Hopkins analyzed some very odd sequences of DNA in the human genome, which were discovered 20 years ago. These don’t match up with those of any ancient hominin species that have already been sequenced, and their origins have been mysterious. But now we have some suspects. One of the strange sequences appears to come from a hominin who mated with us before we ventured out of Africa. The other may come from the great wanderer Homo erectus , who left Africa nearly 2 million years ago and ranged across Asia. Homo erectus may never have encountered Homo sapiens directly, but the researchers suspect that the hominin interbred with the Denisovans before the Denisovans interbred with us. Either way, all of these people—if it is right to call them people—played a role in our species’ story of becoming, yet we are only now learning the nature of that connection. All year, scientists from different fields have been making revisions to the human-origin story. In January, one team announced that they’d found handheld wooden tools along an ancient lakeshore in present-day Greece—a refuge between glaciers where hominins of some kind butchered elephants about 430,000 years ago. These are surely not the first wooden tools ever to be made, but they are the most ancient that we’ve managed to find—and they were used during the Stone Age. That name—“Stone Age”—is misleading. It reveals more about the limits of archeology than about the material culture of the people who lived through the period, who may not have thought of themselves as being defined by stone tools at all. We perceive them that way only because their knapped axes of flint and obsidian are likelier to have survived to the present day than the digging sticks that our forebears smoothed and sharpened. [ Read: When did humans first start wearing clothes? ] Beyond stone and wood, these lakeside elephant butchers likely put all kinds of natural materials to clever use. They may have employed woven twine to sew animal hides together, but we wouldn’t know it, because twine unravels into thin, disintegrating filaments, and bacteria rapidly remove hides from the world. Wood tends to rot away too. In this location, the tools had the good geological fortune to be buried quickly under mud. Stone tools have themselves been reinterpreted. Researchers recently detected traces of poison on an ancient set of quartz arrowheads that were dug up in 1985. The weapons were found in a South African rock shelter that was used by modern humans 60,000 years ago—tens of thousands of years earlier than what had been regarded as the oldest confirmed human use of poison. The ancient South African archers retrieved the neurotoxin from a plant bulb that grows as large as a honeydew melon and dabbed it onto the cold stone of their arrowheads, knowing that it would slow down any animal that they pierced. Some scientists are now calling for a reappraisal of other ancient arrowheads to see whether they too had been sheathed in poison by people whose ingenuity had previously been underestimated by science. Piecing together the history of our species in this way is tedious work, because the evidence is so fragmentary. The Earth’s violent, self-renewing processes erase so much. During the planet’s cold spells, its glaciers steamroll from the poles toward the equator, grinding and scraping whole landmasses clean. In its warmer, middle zones, jungles can sprout up within decades, covering human ruins in a thick and devouring layer of green. Scientists have recently learned that the Amazon rainforest has been concealing millennia-old earthworks on an enormous scale. A team of international researchers spent weeks flying lidar-equipped planes back and forth over a swath of Amazonia. Their laser scans revealed nearly 400 immense structures that were previously unknown to science. From the sky, they saw that these systems of raised banks and deep ditches formed geometrically precise circles, octagons, and squares, and were linked to one another by remarkably straight roads. The earthworks were built 1,200 to 2,500 years ago by the Aquiry civilization. Having surveyed only one small portion of Aquiry territory, the researchers suspect that tens of thousands more of these structures may be waiting silently under the region’s trees. One hundred thousand years from now, the Aquiry ruins might vanish altogether, and in Earth time, 100,000 years is nothing. In 10 million years, even the skyscrapers and continent-sprawling infrastructure of our own civilization will be crushed into sedimentary layers. Nearly everything that we have created will be reduced to trace elements and isotopes, but for a few specimens lucky enough to be fossilized. For all of the other details of our world to persist in human memory, science would need to get better, or civilization itself would need to keep existing, and telling its own story, from now until then.

items.title: A Culture War in the Bedroom
items.description: In the new film I Want Your Sex , characters are action figures in a staging of generational war. On one side is Gen Z, its members portrayed as anxious little prudes. Twenty-three-year-old Elliot is bumbling and directionless. His high-achieving girlfriend is far more interested in studying than she is in him. (When he tries to initiate intimacy, she accuses him of “constantly draining my qi energy.”) His best friend, Apple, is angsty about her lack of interesting life experience—yet she almost always seems to be home, donning pimple cream and loungewear. None of them is having much sex. Their Millennial foil is Erika Tracy: self-serving, insensitive, and ostentatiously sex-positive. She’s a visual artist who has hired a league of underpaid Zoomer assistants—including Elliot—mostly to chew gum and then affix it to a giant drawing of a vagina. She has said publicly that a one-night stand “knows you better than your mother or your best friend ever will.” And she has no problem crossing lines. Amused by Elliot’s innocent skittishness, she promptly suggests that they make their relationship sexual. Soon she’s handcuffing him and making him crawl on the ground. In the bedroom as in the office, she’s dominant and he’s submissive. The film, directed by Gregg Araki, is hitting theaters at a time when many commentators (okay, myself included) are writing nervously about the “sex recession” and the “ romance slump ,” wringing their hands about why the youths aren’t getting laid. Some paint young people as coddled and fragile, too timid to put themselves out there. Meanwhile, many Zoomers point out that they’re not growing up in the same world that older cohorts did: They have plenty of valid reasons to feel inhibited (a pandemic, a housing crisis, a culture of constant digital surveillance ) and plenty of other priorities (saving, studying, worrying). Araki sketches each generation with a cartoonishly broad brush. But the caricatures help illuminate what each perspective might get a little bit right. In an era of shifting etiquette and vigilance against inappropriate behavior, the film seems to ask, can sex be liberating, transgressive, and respectful all at once? [ Read: Too scared for sex ] I Want Your Sex knows that a person’s most intimate experiences can be shaped by their historical context. At first, the choice to make Erika a 30-something struck me as odd; Millennials, who’ve partnered later and less than prior generations, were the ones who kicked off the sex recession. But although they may have been having less sex in their 20s on average, they were also known as the “hookup generation.” Compared with older cohorts, Millennials were more tolerant of gay and premarital sex, and more likely to report having casual sex. And they enjoyed a culture of relative erotic frankness and optimism. Araki, who is 66, grew into adulthood during the AIDS epidemic. In his 20s, he said in a 2023 interview , he felt as if “this black cloud of doom is hanging over you every fucking day.” By the time Millennials were coming of age, some of that darkness had lifted. The HIV pre-exposure drug Truvada was approved for use in 2012, when the median Millennial was about 24. The internet opened up access to information about sexual health and kink. Last year, Match Group’s Singles in America poll crowned Millennials “the horniest generation”: Of all the cohorts surveyed, they reported the highest levels of sexual desire and the most boredom with “vanilla sex.” Erika is, in her way, a perfect encapsulation of the Millennial sex paradox: She has made the erotic a major part of her identity. But it’s not clear that she’s happier for it, or that she’s scratching whatever itch she has—one that might be more existential than physiological. “Sex is everything; it forges us as human beings,” she lectures Elliot. Later, when he reminds her of this, she amends that point: “Sex is everything. It’s also nothing.” If more Zoomers are openly questioning the value of intimacy, perhaps it’s because they’ve picked up on some of that quiet ambivalence. And in the time since Millennials entered adulthood, the rules and expectations about sex have gotten even more complicated. The MeToo movement heightened people’s suspicion of uneven and potentially exploitative power dynamics—perhaps especially in the workplace, one of the primary places where romantic partners used to meet. After decades of relaxing societal norms regarding what’s appropriate to talk about and with whom, backlash arrived in the form of “boundaries” : a suddenly ubiquitous pop-psychology concept. And then COVID hit. By the time Americans emerged from isolation, many were socially rusty and fond of a good night in. The gaps between people aren’t generally getting easier to bridge. [ Read: The great romance slump ] Yet the idea of Zoomer sexlessness seems to have galvanized even just slightly older people to champion eroticism. In one slightly on-the-nose scene in the film, Erika confronts Elliot about what she sees as his age group’s failure of joie de vivre, in sex and in general. “Gen Z is all about FOMO, and yet you’re willing to miss out on the sexual prime of your life?” she asks. He replies earnestly about spending formative years amid a pandemic: “My peers have not been well served growing up in a time where nothing feels safe.” That’s what Erika thinks is the problem with his generation’s risk aversion, though. Why is feeling safe their overarching goal? “Being outside your comfort zone,” she tells him, “is the whole fucking point.” I Want Your Sex isn’t an anti-MeToo movie; it takes manipulations and abuses seriously enough to show that Erika is, at some points, truly acting egregiously. But you also get the sense that she’s right about a few things. Elliot wants to let go of some control. He enjoys a lot of what happens between them. And what he doesn’t enjoy, the movie insinuates, he’ll learn from. Araki seems to be grieving a bygone era: one that felt a little looser, a little spicier, and perhaps more resilient. At one point, when Erika is encouraging Elliot to lighten up, she gives him a copy of Harold Robbins’s Never Love a Stranger , a raunchy novel that became the subject of an obscenity trial in 1949. Certain progressive impulses, the film suggests, somehow led the nation in a big loop—right back to a puritanical streak in which pleasure is seen as threatening enough to suppress. In a perfect sensual landscape, everyone would feel safe and free all at once. I Want Your Sex doesn’t identify the secret to making that happen, of course—and the film arguably avoids the trickiest parts of its own debate by making Erika’s character a woman. Araki has said that the original script featured a young female intern and her male boss, but “after MeToo, I was like, I kind of don’t want to have a male dragging a female around by the hair.” Still, by focusing on BDSM, he offers an alternative framework for navigating desire. The practice inherently involves power differences—but also a code of ethics. When I talked with Yehuda Duenyas, the film’s intimacy coordinator, he drew an analogy between kink etiquette and his own work: Having a clear permission structure and good communication from the start means that people might actually feel more able to lean into passion; they’re not worrying in the moment about what’s acceptable or desired, because they’ve already established it. His job isn’t to make people feel comfortable. It’s to foster clarity and openness. Erika and Elliot don’t exactly model a healthy dynamic. But the film makes a point of emphasizing his agency, even at his most vulnerable. When an incident brings Elliot to an interrogation room to be questioned about his relationship with Erika—don’t ask why—he tells police that he was “way over my head” and “under her control.” And how does he feel about that? Thankful.

items.title: Hard-Luck Men in Hardscrabble Towns
items.description: “I ’m the first writer in the family,” the novelist Richard Russo once said, “but I’m not the first bullshitter in the family.” That honor belonged to his divorced father, Jim, a highway worker with no interest in books and an only intermittent interest in his son. Jim’s strongest connections were with his buddies at the bar. On summer breaks from college, Russo returned to Gloversville, in upstate New York, and his dad would get him on the road crew. When work ended, they would head home, hitting pubs along the way. At each stop, Jim would regale the regulars with a story about something that had happened on the job that day. “He would pay attention to what worked in Roadhouse A,” Russo said in 2025, “so that when he got to Roadhouse B, he would remember what got a laugh and what didn’t, and so he would change the story.” Jim would tell the same story over many days, cutting and shaping, finding the beats. “There’s a word for that,” Russo said. “It’s called revision.” [ From the April 2022 issue: Richard Russo on his father, the fool ] Revision , a refined term that Jim would never have used, is a staple of M.F.A. programs, such as the one his son attended at the University of Arizona. When Russo graduated in 1980, the experimental fiction of William Gass and Kurt Vonnegut was in vogue, but he much preferred the shambling shaggy-dog novels of Twain and Dickens, whose humor arose not from formal innovation but from the foibles of flawed characters (like his dad), many of them poor and unlettered (ditto). Early on, Russo threw in his lot with Tom and Huck and Jim, with David Copperfield and Oliver Twist—characters whose humble beginnings offer a vantage from which to see the absurdity of an unjust world. Beginning with the 1986 publication of his first novel, Mohawk , Russo has filled 10 novels, plus many essays and short stories, with portraits of men born with few gifts save their wits , making their way in an economy not set up to reward their kind. The bulk of his fiction is set in New York, in towns like Gloversville, where the good jobs have vanished (the glove-making trade there—once responsible for 90 percent of gloves sold in America—was by the 1950s already being replaced by imports ). In these places, it’s unclear who is slinging more bull, the semi-employed men in bars or the educated civic “leaders,” such as mayors and bankers, promising that good times will return. In Russo’s best work, especially his classic trilogy, set in fictional North Bath— Nobody’s Fool (1993), Everybody’s Fool (2016), and Somebody’s Fool (2023)—his characters’ banter, crude and self-knowing, reminds us that the worst effects of the modern economy are present not in the landscape but in the soulscape, the fractured lives and identities of obsolete workers. Their barroom bravado is a front, masking inner hurt, or just bewilderment. In the novelist’s business of exploring what’s inside people’s heads—the way we all think more than we can say—Russo is the peer of Jonathan Franzen and Meg Wolitzer , even if his characters think in fewer syllables. At 77, Russo has published a new novel, Under the Falls , that at first seems to be a break with his past work. The characters are young, mostly in their mid‑30s, and the protagonist, Tyler Sinclair, is honest-to-goodness rich. After high school, he left Stone Mountain, another of Russo’s fictional upstate hamlets, riding his guitar to stardom. When he blew out of town, he left behind a toxic love triangle and a paralyzed buddy, the victim of a near drowning that many blamed Tyler for. In the years since, he has milked the town, and a Mellencamp-like image as a boy from the sticks, for songwriting material. Now Tyler has come back to a place he never wanted to see again. Stone Mountain’s denizens feel the same way about him. At his much-ballyhooed return show, he and his band are pelted with eggs. On the way out of town, the band’s limousine is mysteriously driven off the road, and during his convalescence in Stone Mountain, Tyler gets caught up in local intrigue involving dope dealing, manslaughter, and police corruption. Under the Falls is a short potboiling book, lacking the finer-grained mind reading and social texture that Russo excels at (the acknowledgments note that it began as a TV-pilot script). Yet in the Russo tradition, it’s about a boy whose hometown has mired him in grief but also given him the stories that will lift him out of it. And tucked into its harebrained (if thoroughly enjoyable) plotting is a line that could well be Russo’s artistic credo. Tyler is relieved, and a bit amazed, to see how Doc, his paralyzed friend, has made a decent life for himself, with his own trailer, wheelchair, and car (a hearse tricked out with hand controls), funded by his “vast criminal enterprise.” “As an artist,” Russo writes, “Tyler has more than once wondered whether, under the right circumstances, or maybe the wrong ones, simply living life might qualify as art, and it occurs to him that his duty here is simple: to surrender his reservations and simply admire the man.” Among all the hard-luck men in these hardscrabble towns, the ones who compound their bad luck with bad choices interest Russo the most. His emblematic figure is Donald “Sully” Sullivan, the star of the North Bath trilogy, a saga about one man surfing the arc of the 20th century that invites comparison to Richard Ford’s Frank Bascombe books and John Updike’s Rabbit quartet, also anchored by troubled male protagonists. But Sully, whom we first meet in late middle age as a handyman with a bum knee—flashbacks fill in his tortured boyhood, his high-school-football career, his World War II service, his failed marriage—is on the opposite side of the class divide from those men. Bascombe is a writer, then a real-estate agent, and Harry “Rabbit” Angstrom dies rich, fat on sales from the car dealership he inherited from his father-in-law. Sully never has a penny extra until his old age, when he has some luck with the ponies and then inherits his landlady’s decaying house—and discovers how disconcerted he is by the taste of middle-class life. “He’d always suspected that life’s deck was stacked in favor of those with means,” Russo writes. Now what? For Rabbit and Bascombe, the American dream is real, or real enough. For Sully, the idea that he was “now and forevermore insulated against adversity” just doesn’t compute; it feels like a cruel joke. And for Russo, the place that Sully inhabits is at least as interesting as the man himself—a signature of his fiction, which specializes in ensemble novels. “One of the good things about small towns,” Russo writes in his Pulitzer Prize winner, Empire Falls (2001), set in a postindustrial Maine hamlet, “was that they accommodated just about everyone; the lame and disfigured were all your neighbors, and seeing them every day meant that after a while you stopped noticing what made them different.” The important thing is how they’re alike on the inside. In his sad-sack locales, characters face their predicaments with a mix of resilience, disappointment, and humor. They want love or connection, but they need money. Equipped with mostly meager educations and varying degrees of sophistication, they bounce off one another like bumper cars, everyone’s actions affecting everyone else’s. Gainful employment is in short supply; vices take hold, whether ugly addictions or minor gambling habits; and in Under the Falls , the criminality moves beyond small-time hustles. Russo’s townsfolk do one another the courtesy, when necessary, of pretending not to see what’s in front of them; they also fight, make up, make love, and, above all, tolerate one another. We tend to think that, in hollowed-out towns such as the ones Russo writes about, those left behind are left behind in the apocalyptic sense: The chosen ones got raptured out, to better places with more work, more Starbucks, more Subarus. But Russo shows how anyplace is good enough if you’ve chosen it, or can tell yourself that you have. Class and cultural divides are sources of tension, but also of local cohesion, as Tyler discovers in Stone Mountain—and as Sully has known all his life. Just because Sully never went to college doesn’t mean he couldn’t have hacked it. North Bath is always suffering intruders, from downstate and especially from nearby Schuyler Springs—an obvious stand-in for Saratoga Springs, which has the college (Skidmore), the racetrack, the tourist season, and hence the money that Gloversville lacks. Sometimes these interlopers want to buy and rehab a house, and that’s where Sully is indispensable. He and a partner do the fixing up on fixer-uppers. They just want to be paid, with money and perhaps a modicum of respect. After Miles Anderson, a university professor from downstate, keeps him waiting for an hour to talk about some repairs on his new property, Sully gets huffy, leading Anderson to ask, pissily, if Sully wants the work or not. “ ‘Look, Mr. Anderson,’ Sully said, ‘I need the work. I’m just too old to jump up and down, okay? Inside, I’m all aflutter. Trust me.’ ” (The “aflutter” is a nice touch, hinting at the elevated vocabulary Sully can deploy when he wants to.) “ ‘Hmmm,’ Miles Anderson mused. ‘Well, I was also told you were insolent, though I suppose that’s to be expected. The gruff, frontier independence of the American blue-collar worker and all that.’ ” [ From the 2006 Fiction Issue: Richard Russo’s short story “Horseman” ] The only thing worse than new wealth threatening to intrude is old wealth that has fled, leaving desolation. In Empire Falls , there are perennial rumors about what might become of the old mill—is it true that investors from Boston have plans for it? The prologue to Under the Falls features a moving paean to the long-shuttered Stone Mountain Amusement Park. “Remember what amusement parks were like before they became corporate,” Russo writes, “before there were special lines for people who have more money than you do.” For Russo, amusement parks, with their rides and buffets and dining-room windows “left open to capture the breeze off the lake,” were once the great levelers, places where, for a day, “you’re not poor; you’re rich.” Stone Mountain Amusement Park offers an echo of the Ultimate Escape Fun Park, planned by Texas moneymen, that the town banker in Nobody’s Fool hopes to lure to North Bath. But the Texans, after flirting with North Bath, ultimately choose a more prosperous site, near Portland, Maine. It seems they were full of it all along. Russo never intimates that his bullshitters in the roadhouse are better men than the ones in the C-suite, or the ones with tenure, or the rock stars. (He is especially withering, though, about the tenured bullshitters, the professoriat. His most beloved book may well be Straight Man , a campus satire in the tradition of Kingsley Amis and David Lodge.) There’s good and bad everywhere, and Russo is alert to self-serving delusions wherever they surface. “I made a man’s mistakes,” Sully’s absentee father, “Big Jim” (obviously named for Russo’s own father), says at the end of his life. That has the ring of nobility, until we remember that his manly mistakes included beating his family, cheating on his wife, and drinking away his pay. Nor is it lost on the reader that he got away with his malign hijinks because, as a big man in a small town, he knew everyone, was enabled by everyone: cops, neighbors, co-workers. In Under the Falls , the town sheriff knows about, and indirectly profits from, Doc’s drug running. He doesn’t approve, but in a small town, complicity is hard to avoid. Here’s what characters like Sully come to understand about hometowns, at least in their wiser moments, and what Tyler has to learn: Achieving escape velocity is one of those aspirations, like being “now and forevermore insulated against adversity,” that is forever out of reach. “It kind of feels like you’re on the clock,” Tyler reflects about his unexpected wealth and success. “Like any day now somebody’s going to notice there’s been a mistake, after which you’ll go back to being poor.” Which doesn’t mean you should simply stay put. Russo found Gloversville claustrophobic, as did his eccentric mother, whose mental illness—the subject of his 2012 memoir, the aptly titled Elsewhere —was surely exacerbated by being a dreamy, literate soul in a town of Babbitts. The two of them had to get out (Russo’s overattached mom followed him to college in Arizona), only to realize that the fight was never with the town but with themselves. After years of attempting to make a life elsewhere, she returned to Gloversville. So did her son, of course. He never really left. * Illustration source images: Knopf / Ulf Andersen / Getty; David Troncoso / Getty; Chronicle / Alamy; Bettmann / Getty. This article appears in the September 2026 print edition with the headline “Bad Luck, Bad Choices.”
